source: Walsh, McGovern, Clark, O'Connell (2020) Evaluating the neurophysiological evidence for predictive processing as a model of perception
finding: Many studies find the expectation effects predicted by predictive processing, but a significant group failed to replicate them. Detection rate differs by method: global measures versus direct neuron recordings.
numbers: No pooled effect size. Review organised around four hypotheses (error signalling, prediction, distinct prediction and error neurons, hierarchy).
quote: a significant contingent failed to replicate these effects
limits: Paradigms differ a lot (how expectation is learned, passive or attended, informed or not), so cross-study comparison is weak. PP makes different predictions for each variant.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'errors go up the hierarchy' as settled fact. Use it as a loose design metaphor, not as a source of empirical rules.

source: Walsh, McGovern, Clark, O'Connell (2020) Evaluating the neurophysiological evidence for predictive processing as a model of perception
finding: Repetition suppression is explained just as well by plain neural adaptation. The real test is whether expectation, not repetition, causes the suppression. Summerfield and colleagues found expected repeats gave smaller fusiform face area BOLD than unexpected repeats.
numbers: Key controlled test: expected vs unexpected repeats in fusiform face area (fMRI). Later fMRI, MEG and EEG studies are mixed.
limits: Adaptation can be added to feedforward models, so suppression alone does not discriminate theories.
agent_relevance: Any 'prediction error' signal in an LLM trace needs a control for simple repetition or frequency.

source: Walsh, McGovern, Clark, O'Connell (2020) Evaluating the neurophysiological evidence for predictive processing as a model of perception
finding: Attention is a key moderator. Some studies find expectation suppression is abolished without attention. Others find attention boosts predicted and unpredicted stimuli equally. Hsu et al. found predicted vs mispredicted showed no attention effect, but predicted vs unpredicted reversed with attention.
numbers: Three result patterns across studies: interaction model, abolished suppression, equal boost.
limits: Unpredicted and mispredicted are different baselines and give opposite conclusions.
agent_relevance: Baseline choice changes the answer. In agent audits, separate 'no prediction' from 'wrong prediction'.

source: Walsh, McGovern, Clark, O'Connell (2020) Evaluating the neurophysiological evidence for predictive processing as a model of perception
finding: Mouse V1 imaging (Fiser et al. 2016, layer 2/3) found two neuron groups that look like prediction units and error units. Omitting the expected grating gave a strong V1 response that tracked prior predictive activity. Predictive activity was stronger where the grating was reliably stable.
numbers: Calcium imaging, mice in a virtual tunnel, oriented gratings A and B. Spratling showed a division-based error model fits the rodent data better than the subtraction models of Rao-Ballard and Keller.
limits: One lab and species. Simple gratings, which are the stimuli where PP dynamics are mostly reported.
agent_relevance: Supports precision weighting (reliable context gives stronger prediction). Idea for agent: weight a prior by how stable the context has been.

source: Walsh, McGovern, Clark, O'Connell (2020) Evaluating the neurophysiological evidence for predictive processing as a model of perception
finding: Evidence for a prediction-error hierarchy across contiguous levels is scarce. Most PP-like dynamics in V1 come from simple stimuli. For complex stimuli like faces, it is unclear what low-level prediction exists. Authors say good evidence for a hierarchy with descending context, but not specifically a PP inferential hierarchy.
numbers: Hypothesis 4 verdict: evidence 'scarcer'. Cites studies that struggle to show effects across adjacent levels.
limits: Authors note the difficulty of testing is part of the reason. Not proof the theory is false.
agent_relevance: The multi-level 'errors flow up' picture is the least supported part. Do not build a multi-layer error-passing scaffold on neuroscience grounds.

source: Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2021) Predictive coding: a theoretical and experimental review
finding: Expectation suppression and repetition suppression are well established at single-unit level but also explained by neural adaptation. fMRI region-level results are mixed, with both increases and decreases. PC does not clearly predict region-level activity because error neurons drop but value neurons may rise and precision may boost errors.
numbers: Qualitative review, no pooled numbers.
limits: Predictions for aggregate BOLD are unclear, so tests are hard to read in either direction.
agent_relevance: Confirms the theory is hard to falsify at the aggregate level; treat claims of confirmation with care.

source: Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2021) Predictive coding: a theoretical and experimental review
finding: Searching for separate error neurons is not conclusive. Some PC variants use multicompartment neurons with apical dendrites storing errors, so not finding explicit error units would not refute PC. Negative errors need separate positive and negative populations or antagonistic coding.
numbers: Review of implementation variants (Sacramento 2018, Takahashi 2020, Keller and Mrsic-Flogel 2018).
limits: Flexibility means the theory is hard to refute.
agent_relevance: Falsifiability problem: rival tests are weak, so 'works as a metaphor' is the honest status.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Predictive coding approximates backprop along arbitrary computation graphs
finding: Predictive coding converges to exact backprop gradients on arbitrary graphs using local rules. Built PC versions of CNN, RNN and LSTM that match backprop on SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100.
numbers: Exact gradients reached within 100 inference iterations at inference rate 0.1. About 100x compute overhead versus backprop for the CNN. Small CNN (6 and 16 filters, FC 200-150-10), no augmentation, 5 seeds, batch 64.
limits: Small networks, below state of the art, no hyperparameter search. Authors say scaling to resnets and transformers 'should be straightforward'. Later benchmark shows it is not.
agent_relevance: Shows PC is a learning algorithm equivalent to backprop, not a different way of reasoning. Nothing here for a prompt-level scaffold.

source: Pinchetti et al. (2025) Benchmarking predictive coding networks, made simple (ICLR)
finding: Large benchmark of PC networks with the PCX library. PC is comparable to backprop up to depth 7 (VGG-5, VGG-7) but falls behind for deeper models. Best PC results all come from VGG-5. Trend VGG5 > VGG7 > VGG9 > ResNet-18 for PC; the opposite for backprop.
numbers: CIFAR-10 test accuracy. VGG-5: PC-CE 86.61, centered nudging 89.47, backprop-CE 88.11. VGG-9: PC-CE 78.12, backprop-CE 89.18. ResNet-18: PC-CE 43.19, best PC (iPC) 70.44, backprop-CE 92.83. Tiny ImageNet top-1 ResNet-18: PC-CE 9.52 vs backprop-CE 58.00.
quote: the performance of deeper models lag behind
limits: Single library; hyperparameters tuned per method. Row labels in the PDF text were read by position; check the original table before reuse.
agent_relevance: Hierarchy depth hurts PC. Deeper stacks of 'error passing' degrade, which matches keeping layer counts small in a scaffold.

source: Pinchetti et al. (2025) Benchmarking predictive coding networks, made simple (ICLR)
finding: Why depth fails: energy (error) is badly balanced across layers. With state learning rate 0.01 the first hidden layer has about 6 orders of magnitude less energy than the last layer, giving exponentially small gradients. Raising the state rate to 1 balances energy but gives much worse accuracy. AdamW becomes unstable for wide layers.
numbers: Energy ratio first vs last layer about 1e-6 at rate 0.01; about equal at rate 1 (worse accuracy). Widths tested 32 to 4096.
limits: Diagnosis, not a fix.
agent_relevance: Error signals decay across many hops. In a multi-step agent, corrections far from the output carry little signal unless rebalanced.

source: Pinchetti et al. (2025) Benchmarking predictive coding networks, made simple (ICLR)
finding: Speed and method ranking. PCX takes about 5.5 s per CIFAR-100 epoch versus about 110 s reported by a prior implementation. Incremental PC (iPC) is best on small nets but weak on large ones.
numbers: iPC best on MNIST (98.45) and FashionMNIST (89.90). VGG-7 CIFAR-10: iPC 80.15 vs backprop-CE 88.60. ResNet-18 CIFAR-10: iPC 70.44.
limits: Method rankings flip with scale.
agent_relevance: Small-benchmark wins do not transfer to large models.

source: Salvatori et al. (2024) A stable, fast and fully automatic learning algorithm for predictive coding networks (iPC, ICLR)
finding: Incremental PC changes only the weight-update schedule and is more stable. On small language models: masked LM test perplexity iPC 106.19 vs backprop 120.02 vs standard PC 523.08. Conditional LM: iPC 142.54, backprop 113.32, PC 206.34.
numbers: Masked LM: 10 of 10 iPC seeds converged, 7 of 10 backprop, 3 of 10 standard PC. Conditional LM: iPC 7 of 10 converged. AlexNet CIFAR-10 with augmentation: BP 83.12, PC 71.99, iPC 80.11. CNN CIFAR-10: BP 69.34, PC 70.84, iPC 72.54.
quote: iPC constantly performs better than the original formulation
limits: Small models. The paper text states the conditional-LM comparison as '113 vs 143'; the table shows backprop better there.
agent_relevance: Very small LM scale only. No evidence PC training helps a deployed LLM.

source: Pinchetti et al. (2022) Predictive coding beyond Gaussian distributions
finding: Gaussian PC cannot handle transformer layers. Using categorical distributions for attention layers, PC reaches comparable perplexity to backprop on a small conditional language model.
numbers: 1B Word Benchmark, 200,000 train and 10,000 dev instances, length 32, vocab 8001, one block, one head, hidden 128. Test perplexity: backprop 162.64, proposed PC 175.90, Gaussian PC 590.08 (order of rows read from text).
limits: Tiny single-block transformer. Gap of about 8 percent to backprop.
agent_relevance: Predictive-coding training is far from LLM scale.

source: Alonso, Krichmar, Neftci (2023) Understanding and improving optimization in predictive coding networks
finding: Inference learning (PC) needs memory-heavy optimizers like Adam to avoid poor local minima, is computationally heavy, and its speedups over backprop are not robust or well understood. They add a cheaper implementation and a new optimizer.
numbers: Abstract-level claims; computing and memory tables in the paper not extracted.
limits: Skimmed, not every table read.
agent_relevance: Reinforces that the training claims are fragile to optimizer choice.

source: Caucheteux, Gramfort, King (2023) Evidence of a predictive coding hierarchy in the human brain listening to speech (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: Adding embeddings of future words to GPT-2 activations improves brain mapping. Best forecast distance is 8 words (about 3.15 s). Frontal and parietal areas forecast farther ahead and at deeper, more contextual layers than temporal areas.
numbers: fMRI, 304 listeners, Narratives dataset, 27 stories 7 to 56 min, 4.6 h unique. GPT-2 layer 8 best brain score R=0.23 in superior temporal sulcus, 60% of noise ceiling. Forecast gives 23 percent (SD 9 across individuals) gain. Inferior frontal gyrus d* higher than anterior STS by 0.9 words (SE 0.2, P<0.001). Optimal depth difference angular vs Heschl 2.5 layers (SE 0.3).
quote: brain makes predictions over multiple timescales
limits: Correlational, linear encoding. Depth differences small on average. The hierarchy is of forecast range, not of error messages.
agent_relevance: One measured link between multi-timescale prediction and LLM layers. Supports using different prediction horizons at different abstraction levels.

source: Antonello and Huth (2024) Predictive coding or just feature discovery? An alternative account of why language models fit brain data (Neurobiol Lang)
finding: Rival explanation. Next-word prediction ability correlates with brain fit (replicated), but general transfer to other representations explains it equally well. Within a model, representations best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations.
numbers: 97 representations from NLP models, 5 subjects (fMRI). Correlation of encoding performance with next-word prediction r=0.847; with general transfer r=0.864 (not significantly different).
quote: does not uniquely (or even best) explain
limits: Highly collinear metrics, so the authors say transfer is not proven either.
agent_relevance: Brain-LLM alignment does not prove prediction is the key objective. Do not cite it as support for prediction-error scaffolds.

source: Heilbron, Armeni, Schoffelen, Hagoort, de Lange (2022) A hierarchy of linguistic predictions during natural language comprehension (PNAS)
finding: GPT-2 word surprise modulates brain responses, with an N400-like negative peak near 400 ms. Prediction signatures for syntax category, phonemes and semantics are dissociable, and word-level predictions inform phoneme-level predictions.
numbers: EEG: 19 participants, 1 h of audiobook; cluster test p=2e-4. MEG: 3 participants, 9 h, individual head casts.
quote: brain spontaneously predicts upcoming language at multiple levels
limits: Only 3 MEG participants. Statistics use model-derived surprise as a proxy for the brain's own prediction.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support for top-down prediction across levels in language, measured with an LLM.

source: Song et al. (2024) Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation (Nat Neurosci)
finding: Prospective configuration: neurons settle activity first, then weights change. In predictive coding networks this reduces interference, learns faster with small batches, resists catastrophic forgetting, and adapts faster under concept drift versus backprop. Also fits human and animal learning data.
numbers: Tests: FashionMNIST two-task forgetting, CIFAR-10 CNN, concept drift, few-example learning, RL. Batch size 1 shows a clear gap (exact values not extracted).
limits: Small networks and standard benchmarks. Exact margins not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Idea: settle the whole picture first, then update. Analogue is rethinking before committing a plan edit.

source: Evaluating the compatibility of predictive coding as a model of linguistic predictability (2026, Front Cogn)
finding: Many predictability effects in reading fit PC: N400 context effects and faster reading. The frontal positivity to plausible violations, and brain-behaviour dynamics in natural reading, are hard to reconcile. PC likely is not the sole core mechanism of language.
numbers: Four hypotheses tested: error, top-down prediction, plausibility, hierarchy. Narrative review.
quote: likely does not reflect the sole core mechanism
limits: Review, no pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: PC explains part of language, not all. Use as one mechanism among others.

source: Cross-domain probabilistic cueing study (2025) Multimodal evidence challenges the effectiveness of probabilistic cueing
finding: With 75 percent valid cues, expectation did not change the fidelity of sensory representations. Visual expectancy had behavioural effects (error, guess rate) but no neural or pupil sensory-fidelity effect. Motor/temporal expectancy effect was feature-unspecific.
numbers: n=51 final (58 recruited), EEG plus pupil. Response error: visual F(1,51)=16.996, partial eta2=0.250, BF10=245; motor F=5.219, BF10=1.75. Reproduction precision: null, BF10 about 0.16 for both. Guess rate: visual eta2=0.209.
quote: questioning the effectiveness of probabilistic cueing paradigms
limits: Student sample (7 of 51 male), one paradigm. Authors say it adds to doubts about cueing paradigms.
agent_relevance: Stated expectations help behaviour but do not obviously sharpen representations. Hints are not the same as internal predictions.

source: Rao and Ballard (1999) Predictive coding in the visual cortex
finding: Founding model: higher areas send predictions down, lower areas send residual errors up. A trained hierarchical network reproduced end-stopping and other extra-classical receptive field effects.
numbers: From memory and citation in the reviews read; exact numbers not checked this session.
limits: Not opened. Model reproduces effects with simple stimuli. Walsh review notes alternative accounts.
agent_relevance: Origin of the metaphor only.

source: Kok, Jehee, de Lange (2012) Less is more: expectation sharpens representations in the primary visual cortex
finding: Expected stimuli reduced V1 BOLD amplitude yet improved stimulus decoding (sharpening). Often cited as evidence for prediction.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: Later cueing study (b20) fails to show sharpened representations with 75 percent cues.
agent_relevance: Low signal does not mean low information.

source: Whittington and Bogacz (2017) An approximation of the error backpropagation algorithm in a predictive coding network
finding: Early result that a PC network with local Hebbian rules approximates backprop. Cited in the reviews read.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Superseded by exact equivalence (Millidge 2020).
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Schrimpf et al. (2021) The neural architecture of language: integrative modeling converges on predictive processing (PNAS)
finding: Models that predict the next word better also predict human neural and behavioural data better. Replicated by Antonello and Huth (b16) across 97 representations (r=0.847).
numbers: Not opened; see b16 for the replication number.
limits: Alternative explanation (shared general features) not excluded.
agent_relevance: Same caution as b16.

source: Keller and Mrsic-Flogel (2018) Predictive processing: a canonical cortical computation
finding: Reviews mouse evidence for error and prediction neurons; proposes positive and negative error unit populations (described in Walsh and Millidge reviews). Spratling later showed a division-based model fits rodent data better.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Details from secondary reading only.
agent_relevance: Signpost.

source: Feuerriegel, Vogels, Kovacs (2021) Evaluating the evidence for expectation suppression and its role in predictive coding
finding: Review arguing expectation suppression is hard to attribute to prediction error and may reflect attention or adaptation. Recalled from memory; not opened.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Unverified recall.
agent_relevance: Same limits as Walsh.

source: Alink and Blank (2021) Can expectation suppression be explained by reduced attention to predictable stimuli?
finding: Tested attention as a rival explanation for expectation suppression. Title confirmed in an index search; results not read.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Results unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Candidate for follow-up.
